headline: Jharkhand Voids TDPL’s Exam Ledger
deck: The state cancelled JSSC-CGL and every exam, result and selection tied to TDPL after a 16-day hunger strike. It ordered a CID probe, left the CBI demand unanswered and published no transition for selected candidates.
body: Jharkhand’s special Cabinet meeting on 17 August announced the cancellation of JSSC-CGL and used broader language extending the remedy to examinations, results, selections or candidates and other activities associated with TDPL [E1][E2][E3]. That wording reaches well beyond one disputed examination: on its face, the state proposed to erase the recruitment consequences produced through the company as well as the examinations themselves [E3]. At 23:10 UTC, however, no written Cabinet resolution, gazette or JSSC notification setting out that operative scope was public [E2][E3]. The government therefore announced the deletion before publishing the document that would tell candidates which entries in the ledger had legally disappeared.

Scope matters because an exam cancellation, a voided result and a cancelled selection extinguish different stages of a recruitment process [E2][E3]. The public announcement grouped those stages together, including candidates associated with TDPL, without a published transition rule explaining how the order would treat people whose selection process had advanced further [E3]. No official enumeration of affected candidates or rule for people who had already joined was public by 23:10 UTC [E2][E3]. Until the written instrument appears, the announcement supplies a remedy in broad nouns while leaving its legal edges unstated.

Investigation followed a different jurisdictional track. Chief Minister Hemant Soren ordered the state CID to examine irregularities in examinations held since 2014, and the government also announced a reforms committee under senior official Amitabh Kaushal [E2][E4]. No CBI inquiry was ordered on 17 August, so the central-agency demand that had animated the protest remained unanswered [E2][E3][E4]. Cancellation changes the recruitment ledger; the CID order determines which state investigative body is supposed to inspect how that ledger came to be compromised.

The procurement dispute supplies one reason the state treated TDPL itself as part of the problem. Reporting on the inquiry says the company received some examination work by nomination without participating in a competitive bid, despite having previously been blacklisted by JSSC [E5]. That finding does not establish that every TDPL engagement followed the same procurement route, so the broader contracts cannot be treated as identical [E5]. The narrower fault line is still severe: a firm carrying a prior commission blacklisting was subsequently entrusted with work through a nomination mechanism that bypassed an open contest [E5].

The protest ended only in part. Devendra Nath Mahato ended his 16-day hunger strike at Sadar Hospital after the Cabinet announcement and suspended his protest [E6]. Other representatives of the reform forum continued to press for a CBI investigation, preserving a demand the Cabinet had not granted [E2][E3]. The government had therefore satisfied the cancellation demand strongly enough to end Mahato’s fast while leaving the argument over who should investigate the system unresolved [E2][E3][E6].

Cancellation also produced a constituency on the other side of the remedy. Around 2,000 selected candidates were reported protesting the decision, while no official count of those affected or published transition mechanism accompanied the announcement [E2][E3]. The strongest counter-case for the government is straightforward: wholesale cancellation can protect future recruitment from machinery the state believes has lost public credibility, particularly when the disputed vendor sits inside the examination process [E2][E3][E5]. The cost of acting before publishing the operative text is equally concrete, because candidates who may have done nothing wrong cannot yet determine from a formal instrument which result, selection or appointment interest the state has extinguished [E2][E3].

Jharkhand’s 17 August action therefore combined three remedies that should not be mistaken for one: cancellation of TDPL-linked recruitment activity, a CID investigation reaching back to examinations since 2014, and an administrative reforms committee [E2][E3][E4]. The CBI demand remained outside that package, while the position of selected and already-joined candidates remained undefined in any public written transition rule [E2][E3]. A formal resolution or JSSC order could narrow, sequence or qualify the Cabinet’s oral breadth; until one appears, the announced categories are the only public map of what was cancelled [E2][E3]. The state cancelled a paper trail in public and still owes the paper that says exactly what vanished.
